leads.name: The Copper Beech of the Upper Garden
leads.age_estimate: roughly 205 to 215 years, from the register's planting band of 1810 to 1820

location.address: At the back of the Boventuin, the upper garden of Paleis Het Loo

leads.story:
Copper beeches were a fashion, and this one arrived at the height of it.

The purple-leaved form of the common beech is a natural mutation. It turns up on its own now and then in European woods, and from the eighteenth century onward nurseries learned to graft it and sold it hard to anyone laying out a landscape garden. Between 1810 and 1820, when this one went into the back of the upper garden at Het Loo, having one was a statement about being current.

Two centuries later the fashion has aged into something better. A copper beech at this size is a dark solid mass of a tree, and in a formal garden built on symmetry and pale gravel it does the useful job of being the one heavy dark thing in the composition.

Stand under it rather than in front of it. Beech leaves are thin enough that a mature purple canopy lit from above turns the light underneath a deep red, which is the reason people planted them and the reason the photographs never work.

It is at the far end of the Boventuin, behind the formal planting.
leads.access: Paid. Inside the formal gardens of Paleis Het Loo, covered by a museum ticket.
leads.transport: About 3 km north of Apeldoorn station, bus to Paleis Het Loo.
leads.how_to_recognise: The large dark purple-leaved beech at the back of the upper garden.

best_time.label: October, when the purple turns to copper

leads.removed_reason: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen nr 1685697 (felled years ago, giant polypore fungus) and nr 1685698 (felled 2006, giant polypore) are status 5, Dood/geveld

leads.name: The Copper Beech by the Pond
leads.age_estimate: roughly 175 to 185 years, from the register's planting band of 1840 to 1850

location.address: At the back of the palace garden, west side of the pond, Paleis Het Loo

leads.story:
A generation younger than the beech at the back of the upper garden, and planted where it would be reflected.

This is the second copper beech in these gardens and the placing is the point of it. It stands on the west side of the pond, which means the water sits between you and the tree for most of the approach, and a dark purple canopy over still water is a trick that landscape gardeners had worked out long before anyone here was planting.

The register puts it between 1840 and 1850. By then the copper beech was no longer a novelty and had settled into being a standard part of the vocabulary, the heavy dark accent you put where a composition needs weight.

What two centuries add is bulk that no design anticipated. These trees keep thickening long after they stop rising, so a mature one ends up out of scale with everything planted alongside it, and the garden quietly rearranges itself around the biggest thing in it.

Go on a still morning and look at the water rather than the tree.
